evidence: src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: @Entity('invoices') on class InvoiceEntity maps the class to a database table, which is a persistence (infrastructure) responsibility.
src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') on id makes the database generate the key, which is a persistence (infrastructure) responsibility.
src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: @Column() on orderId and amount maps fields to database columns, which is a persistence (infrastructure) responsibility.
src/invoice/invoice.entity.ts: the class has no domain behaviour or invariants; it only describes an ORM record shape.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The file sits in the domain layer because it matches the **/*.entity.ts pattern. Its only content is a TypeORM persistence mapping. The class is tied to the 'invoices' table, and its fields are marked as database columns and an auto-generated UUID primary key. That is persistence or ORM schema work, which belongs to infrastructure. The class has no domain behaviour, invariants or business rules. It is a database record shape. The rubric names persistence logic in a domain file as a failure. One mitigating point: the layer model files all *.entity.ts files under domain, which may mean the project treats ORM entities as domain models on purpose. No ADR prose confirms this, so the rubric applies as written. Confidence is moderate because of that convention.

violations.message: InvoiceEntity carries persistence mapping that belongs to infrastructure: @Entity('invoices'), @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') on id, and @Column() on orderId and amount. The file is declared domain but its only job is mapping the class to the database. Move the ORM mapping to an infrastructure persistence model, or confirm in an ADR that ORM entities count as domain.
